appraisal_events.evidence: Expecting an extraordinary beauty ("Elle doit être merveilleuse"), Saint-Loup instead reacts to Albertine's photograph with "une stupéfaction qui allait jusqu'à la stupidité," finally asking, half-stunned, "C'est ça la jeune fille que tu aimes ?"
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup's admiring anticipation collapses into bafflement when he actually sees Albertine, revealing to an outside eye an ordinary-looking woman rather than the extraordinary being the narrator's suffering had led him to imagine.

status_effects.explanation: Seen through Saint-Loup's undistorted, outsider eyes, Albertine falls short of the extraordinary figure his prior admiration had led him to expect, deflating her mystique.

Saint-Loup tactfully says nothing but takes on the restrained, slightly disdainful manner one has before a sick man, implicitly treating the narrator's devastation over an ordinary-looking woman as a kind of malady.

ambiguities: Saint-Loup's diminishment of Albertine and implicit view of the narrator as pitiably deluded are conveyed through the narrator's own retrospective analysis rather than direct speech, so the degree to which this reading is Saint-Loup's actual judgment versus the narrator's generalized theory of lovers' distorted perception is not fully separable.
